result:
I'll write about the strange, quiet magic of ordinary moments.

---

There's a particular hour in the late afternoon when light comes through windows at a slant, and dust motes become visible—tiny galaxies suspended in a room. I've noticed that people rarely talk about this. We have words for sunrise and sunset, for golden hour and blue hour, but not for this: the *slant hour*, when everything ordinary becomes briefly luminous.

I think about how much of life happens in these unnamed spaces. The pause before answering a question. The walk to the mailbox when you don't need to go. The way a cat will sit in a sunbeam that has moved three inches since morning, following it across the floor like a slow, furry sundial.

My grandmother used to say that time moves differently when you're bored. I didn't believe her then. Now I think she meant that boredom is the only honest way to experience duration—when you're not trying to fill time, you can actually feel it passing, grain by grain, like sand through fingers you're trying not to close.

There's a tree outside my window that I've watched for three years. I don't know what kind it is. In spring it makes these small white flowers that smell faintly of something I can't name—not sweet exactly, more like the idea of sweetness, or the memory of a smell from childhood. In autumn the leaves turn a color that has no name in any language I know. Not orange. Not yellow. Something between, with a darkness underneath, like a bruise healing.

I used to think I needed to travel to see the world. Now I think the world is mostly here, in this square of sky, this particular quality of afternoon light, the sound of a neighbor's wind chimes that I've learned to hear only when they stop.

The strange thing about attention is that it changes what you're attending to. The tree was always there. The light was always slanting. But now that I've noticed, I can't un-notice. The world has become *thicker*, more present, like a book you've read twice—the second reading slower, stranger, full of things you missed because you were rushing toward the ending.

I don't know where this is going. That's probably the point.

Someone once told me that the Japanese have a word for the sadness of things passing—*mono no aware*. I looked it up and found seventeen different translations, none quite right. This seems appropriate. Some experiences resist being pinned down. They want to remain in motion, in the slant of light, in the space between one moment and the next.

I'm going to go make tea now. The kettle is whistling. There's a particular sound it makes when it's almost ready—not the full boil, but the *approach* to boiling, a kind of promise. I like that sound. I like that I've learned to hear it.

The dust motes are still there, I think. Or new ones. It's hard to tell. They look the same. They are not the same. This is almost everything I know about being alive.

---
